In contrast, decision models (DMs), given a description of the environment and task, can perform well in sparse-reward tasks, but, as they do not learn from reward, they are not able to improve towards the optimal solution. In this paper, we present Decision Model-Guided Training (DMGT), a technique that uses a DM with a description of the environment and task to initialise an RL policy, combining the DM's ability to act without training with RL's ability to improve from reward. Instead of exploring from scratch, the agent reaches the goal and receives reward from its first episodes, and RL then improves its policy beyond what the DM achieves. We demonstrate through experiments on seven tasks that our approach outperforms RL in all seven and DM in five. In addition, we provide comprehensive guidelines, derived from ablation studies, for describing an environment and task to a DM.

Machine Learning.title: Sonar-MoE: In-Backward Expert Updates for Memory-Efficient Mixture-of-Experts Training
Machine Learning.summary: Most parameters of a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model belong to its experts, and standard training keeps every expert gradient in GPU memory until the optimizer step. This memory grows with the number and size of the experts, so it rises as MoE models scale. We introduce Sonar-MoE, which updates each expert tensor during the backward pass and frees its gradient right away. It brings optimizer-in-backward from dense models to batched MoE expert tensors, so the GPU never holds more than one layer of expert gradients. When we fine-tune OLMoE-1B-7B and Granite-3.1-3B-A800M in bf16 with two expert-kernel backends, Sonar-MoE lowers peak memory by 19% to 22%. Its updates are bitwise identical to standard training without expert gradient clipping, and held-out loss stays within 0.003 of all baselines. Each step also takes 17% to 23% less time than standard training with global-norm clipping. Updating whole batched tensors rather than individual experts is what keeps Sonar-MoE fast, as it avoids a 20% to 72% slowdown while using the same memory. Sonar-MoE matches optimizer-in-backward over all parameters in memory and speed while still clipping the dense parameters.

Machine Learning.title: AttnSR: Attention Step Reward for Long-Horizon Agentic RL
Machine Learning.summary: Long-horizon LLM agents make multi-step decisions, yet outcome-reward-only reinforcement learning provides little direct supervision for individual steps. We introduce AttnSR, a step-level reward augmentation method that derives reward allocations from policy attention extracted during training replay, without a separately trained reward model or additional rollouts. AttnSR traces backward through the policy model attention graph to estimate the relevance of earlier steps to the final response. The terminal step, measured relative to a running baseline, determines whether these rewards reinforce or penalize the selected steps. In a controlled Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct study, AttnSR consistently outperforms the PPO baseline across all evaluated checkpoints on ALFWorld, raising final held-out success from 91.2% to 97.1%. The ablation experiment shows that the benefit depends on how intermediate rewards are assigned, rather than simple accumulation of step rewards over time. AttnSR also improves ScienceWorld at every checkpoint while cutting environment interactions by 29.9%. These results support policy attention as a practical prior for step-level reward allocation in long-horizon agentic RL. Code is available at https://github.com/fairyshine/AttnSR .
Machine Learning.comment: 20 pages, 4 figures, including appendices. Code: https://github.com/fairyshine/AttnSR

Machine Learning.title: Flux as a Codec: Zero-Shot Lossy Compression with Flux
Machine Learning.summary: We propose FluxC, a zero-shot codec that uses Flux as a compression prior. Although DiffC has shown that pretrained diffusion models can serve as zero-shot codecs, we ask how the choice of coding path and reconstruction method affects rate--distortion--perception behavior. We analyze FluxC along three axes: coding cost and bit allocation, reconstruction method, and low rate distortion. At matched signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), we show that the path choice does not affect the ideal information rate, but changes how bits are allocated across time steps. For reconstruction, we compare ancestral sampling, one-step ODE reconstruction, and many-step ODE reconstruction. Our analysis shows that ODE-based reconstruction can achieve lower distortion than ancestral sampling, especially in the low rate regime. Experiments on Gaussian sources and natural images support this prediction. Moreover, FluxC performs competitively with, and in some cases outperforms, recent neural image compression methods, suggesting that Flux can serve as a principled zero-shot codec.

Machine Learning.title: Reasoning on the Manifold: Bidirectional Consistency for Self-Verification in Diffusion Language Models
Machine Learning.summary: While Diffusion Large Language Models (dLLMs) offer structural advantages for global planning, efficiently verifying that they arrive at correct answers via valid reasoning traces remains a critical challenge. In this work, we propose a geometric perspective: Reasoning on the Manifold. We hypothesize that valid generation trajectories reside as stable attractors on the high-density manifold of the learned distribution, whereas invalid paths exhibit off-manifold drift. To operationalize this, we introduce Bidirectional Manifold Consistency (BMC), a training-free, unsupervised metric that quantifies the stability of the generated sequence through a forward-masking and backward-reconstruction cycle. Empirically, we demonstrate BMC's versatility across the full reasoning lifecycle: (1) in Diagnosis, it serves as a robust discriminator of solution validity without ground truth answer; (2) in Inference, it enables rejection resampling to effectively concentrate computational resources on complex reasoning tasks; and (3) in Alignment, it functions as a dense geometric reward that transforms sparse outcome supervision into fine-grained guidance, empowering models to self-evolve beyond standard baselines. Our results establish intrinsic geometric stability as a robust indicator of correctness for dLLMs.
Machine Learning.comment: 31 pages, 7 figures. Accepted to the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2026). Camera-ready version

Machine Learning.title: Same Answer, Different Future: Matched Predictions Do Not Imply Matched Belief Updating in Language Models
Machine Learning.summary: Language models can produce similar probabilistic predictions after observing outcomes, reading summaries, receiving instructions, or undergoing activation interventions. Whether these routes induce equivalent belief states remains unclear: agreement in current predictions does not establish how a model will respond to subsequent evidence. We investigate this distinction in a Bernoulli inference task with an analytic Bayesian reference. Across three open-weight language models, we prepare states through four textual routes and two activation-level interventions, measure both next-outcome continuations and explicit probabilistic estimates, and append identical new evidence from each prepared state. We quantify the persistence of the initial belief through its effective evidence weight, the number of new observations it is worth. We find that the format of evidence decides which readouts express its content: outcome sequences primarily affect continuations, whereas summaries and stated rates primarily affect explicit estimates. Moreover, effective weights differ substantially across routes, with summaries receiving weights that scale weakly with their stated observation counts and elicitation questions changing inferred weights by orders of magnitude. In a one-shot steering setting, an intervention that reproduces a natural record's immediate prediction loses most of its effect under subsequent evidence. These results show that agreement in current readouts is insufficient to establish equivalence in belief updating: how a belief is acquired and how it is read jointly determine its subsequent dynamics.

Machine Learning.title: EDGAR: Efficient Diffusion-Driven Gaussian Avatar Refinement via Synthetic Failure
Machine Learning.summary: Recent advances in Gaussian splatting have enabled efficient and photorealistic head avatar reconstruction, yet monocular video-based or image-based methods still suffer from under-constrained geometry and texture, leading to artifacts such as blurring, stretching, and temporal instability. We present EDGAR (Efficient Diffusion-Driven Gaussian Avatar Refinement), a conditional diffusion framework designed to enhance the quality of Gaussian avatars by correcting artifacts while preserving identity fidelity. To train EDGAR, we construct EDGAR-SET, a hybrid triplet dataset composed of real-captured and synthetic-rendered samples, which simulates realistic Gaussian avatar failure cases by pairing degraded renderings with ground-truth and reference images. EDGAR refines degraded frames through a fusion block that injects identity features extracted by the self-supervised Sapiens model into a one-step diffusion backbone, enabling effective artifact removal without sacrificing efficiency. Our EDGAR model incorporates a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture to address diverse degradation types and severity levels. The refined multi-view renderings are subsequently used as pseudo-targets to optimize a single underlying Gaussian avatar, so that the final avatar can be rendered without applying EDGAR to every output frame. Experiments on three different Gaussian avatar reconstruction methods, each evaluated under three different settings, show improvements in both perceptual and reconstruction measures over the raw outputs and an SDEdit-style refinement baseline. In addition, cross-view evaluation demonstrates improved calibrated consistency, while tests under large yaw and open-mouth expressions verify robustness under extreme settings. These results collectively indicate a useful operating regime for recoverable appearance artifacts. The code is available at https://kwanyun.github.io/edgar/
Machine Learning.comment: Accepted to ACM Transactions on Graphics

Machine Learning.title: Cross-Asset Knowledge Transfer for Early Fault Detection of Data-Scarce Assets Without Target Fault Data
Machine Learning.summary: Reliability management of industrial fleets depends on early fault warnings, yet lifecycle data across similar assets are highly imbalanced. A few assets accumulate run-to-failure histories, while newly installed or rarely failing assets provide only normal-condition data. This paper asks how diagnostic knowledge can be transferred from a data-rich source asset to a data-scarce target asset when no fault data have been observed on the target. We formulate cross-asset early fault detection as a zero-shot domain adaptation problem, in which zero-shot refers to the absence of target fault samples, and propose a framework that requires only normal data from the target. The framework comprises (1) a statistical process control step that labels the source asset run-to-failure data with an exponentially weighted moving average chart, reducing manual annotation to verifying flagged segments, (2) an Adapted Domain-Adversarial Neural Network (ADANN) that combines domain-adversarial training and a Maximum Mean Discrepancy penalty with an Adapted Classification-Domain (ACD) loss, which anchors the classifier normal region to the target own normal data, and (3) an ahead-of-time labeling scheme with a prediction horizon that targets incipient faults. Under an exact-classification assumption, a theoretical analysis characterizes the domain-adversarial term for a normal-only target and the alignment state in which source fault features remain separated from target normal features. On a public run-to-failure bearing dataset, ADANN attains the highest mean F1-score among four transfer baselines, with a nominally significant precision gain over the strongest baseline, and its robustness is examined under synthetic noise.

Machine Learning.title: Emergent Generalization by Representation Learning in Artificial Neural Networks
Machine Learning.summary: Dimensionality reduction has proven powerful for identifying neural manifolds, which are low-dimensional structures underlying high-dimensional neural activity. These low-dimensional representations have improved the interpretability of population-level coding. Yet whether such low-dimensional representations are biologically relevant and confer functional advantages in learning systems, or merely reflect neuron-level activity, remains contested in neuroscience. We show that an explicit information bottleneck forcing a recurrent neural network to learn a low-dimensional representation is necessary for rotational and out-of-distribution generalisation in a time-series prediction task. Using information-theoretic measures of causal emergence, we characterise the dynamics of this representation across the memorisation-to-generalisation transition, finding a non-monotonic trajectory which shows an initial decrease, a minimum, and a subsequent rise to a maximum, even as prediction loss falls monotonically. This trajectory scales with task complexity, and the magnitude of emergent structure reliably predicts generalisation performance. Analysis of hippocampal CA1 and medial prefrontal activity in rats learning an alternating maze task reveals analogous non-monotonic emergence dynamics that track behavioural performance. Together, these findings indicate that the ability of neural networks to learn compact, distributed and emergent representations confers a functional advantage for generalisation, supporting a causal role for learned representations in cognition.

Machine Learning.title: Structure from Collision via Hypothesis-Space Reasoning
Machine Learning.summary: Knowledge of the hidden interior structure of an object, including the presence and location of cavities, is essential for predictive simulation, robotic manipulation, and nondestructive inspection. However, such cavities leave no direct signature on the static visible surface, making collision-induced deformation one of the few cues used to infer their presence. Structure from Collision (SfC) addresses this problem by recovering the hidden interior structure of an object from multiview observations of a collision event. SfC is challenging for two reasons: hidden cavities are only indirectly observable through surface motion, and voids correspond to the absence of material, making direct optimization using standard density representations difficult. The density-based SfC baseline inherits both difficulties. Surface-matching gradients do not directly indicate the cavity location, while density gradients can be weak or uninformative inside or near void regions. Therefore, we reformulate SfC as hypothesis-space reasoning, representing hidden cavities as explicit structural hypotheses whose variables encode available structural assumptions rather than relying on implicit density updates. A global stage performs gradient-free optimization over this hypothesis space using forward-only material point method (MPM) simulation. A local stage then refines the selected hypothesis as a Lagrangian particle system through gradient-based optimization using differentiable MPM simulation. On the SfC benchmark, our method improves hidden-structure reconstruction and future prediction over the density-based SfC baseline. Interior-topology stress tests and robustness analyses characterize its scope and limitations. The project page is available at https://www.kecl.ntt.co.jp/people/kaneko.takuhiro/projects/sfc-hypothesis/.

Machine Learning.title: ASAP: Attention Sink Anchored Pruning
Machine Learning.summary: Vision Transformers (ViTs) face severe computational bottlenecks due to the quadratic complexity of self-attention at high resolutions. Existing token reduction methods rely on local metrics -- such as single-layer attention scores -- that are inherently vulnerable to the attention sink phenomenon, where uninformative tokens are paradoxically preserved over salient foreground objects. We propose ASAP (Attention Sink Anchored Pruning), a training-free framework that recasts this sink as a feature. Modeling ViT information flow as a Lazy Random Walk, ASAP identifies the sink as a dominant accumulator of probability mass. By computing the diffusion distance to the sink within the cumulative transition matrix, ASAP partitions tokens via Radial Diffusion Clustering and compresses background redundancy through Transition Weight Pooling in a single shot. Extensive experiments across image, video, and vision-language tasks demonstrate ASAP outperforms state-of-the-art methods, accelerating throughput by up to 48% while maintaining or even exceeding baseline accuracy.

Machine Learning.title: DynSHAP: Towards Explainable Dynamic Survival Analysis
Machine Learning.summary: Deep learning models for dynamic survival analysis (DSA) achieve strong predictive performance by incorporating longitudinal patient data, but their black box nature limits clinical trust and adoption. Existing explainability methods cannot handle longitudinal, irregular inputs and functional survival outputs simultaneously, which limits their usability in DSA. We propose DynSHAP, a SHAP framework suited specifically for dynamic survival analysis. It extends common marginal SHAP estimators to this setting by treating time--feature pairs as players in the Shapley game. We further introduce Temporal DynSHAP, which learns linear dependencies in features over time and uses conditional sampling to address them in explanations. When applied to synthetic data with known ground-truth attributions, Temporal DynSHAP recovers temporally dependent features more accurately than marginal estimators for a given state-of-the-art model. Applied to two real-world clinical datasets and two DSA architectures, DynSHAP produces attributions faithful to model learning, allowing medical experts to see which patient information drove the prediction and when.

Machine Learning.title: DISCERN: Distributional Synthetic Replay for Retain-Free Incremental Machine Unlearning
Machine Learning.summary: Machine unlearning aims to remove the influence of specific training data from a trained model without retraining from scratch. In real deployments, however, deletion requests arrive over time, calling for incremental class unlearning (ICU): classes are removed sequentially, previously forgotten knowledge must remain forgotten, and the remaining classes must be preserved. We present DIstributional SynthetiC rEplay for Retain-free iNcremental unlearning (DISCERN), an intervention-based class unlearning method that replaces access to the retain set with synthetic embeddings sampled from per-class parametric distributions. Unlike prototype-based replay, which assumes an isotropic Gaussian around each class centroid, DISCERN fits Euclidean (Gaussian, Laplace, Student's $t$) and directional (von Mises--Fisher, Fisher--Bingham) families to each class and selects among them through statistical tests and, when none of them accepts, cross-validated log-likelihood. This design is motivated by the architecture-dependent latent geometry: transformer embeddings lie approximately on a hypersphere and concentrate around class directions, unlike those of convolutional networks. We evaluate DISCERN against seven retain-free baselines on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100 with two convolutional and two transformer backbones, under single-class, multi-class, and incremental unlearning. DISCERN is competitive when classes are removed at once and is the most stable method in ICU on transformers: on ViT-B/16, after 20 sequential deletions it retains a harmonic mean of $0.797$, whereas the strongest method in the simultaneous setting drops from $0.918$ to $0.048$. A paired ablation shows that per-class distribution selection substantially reduces the resurfacing of previously forgotten classes, acting as a stabilizer of accumulated forgetting rather than a uniform improvement.

Computation and Language.title: $D^2$-OPD: Separating Direction and Distance in Extrapolative On-Policy Distillation
Computation and Language.summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student model to match a teacher's next-token distributions on student-generated prefixes. Extrapolative OPD further extends the teacher's log-probability shift relative to a reference policy to construct stronger learning targets. However, existing methods couple extrapolation direction and distance, allowing the magnitude of the teacher's shift to dictate how far the target moves. We propose $D^2$-OPD, decoupling these two factors: a per-prefix hard KL constraint bounds the target's distance from the teacher, while an adaptive combination of the teacher's post-training shift and the initial student--teacher gap determines the extrapolation direction. We optimize the student toward this target using forward KL, providing learning signals even for low-probability tokens. We evaluate three settings: where standard OPD performs well, where it struggles with base-model initialization, and where no teacher reference is available. On mathematical reasoning benchmarks, $D^2$-OPD attains the highest score in all three settings, outperforming the strongest baseline by up to 9.45 points. Ablations validate the contributions of each component.

Computation and Language.title: How Do AI Agents Waste Your Money?
Computation and Language.summary: AI agents may consume massive tokens across a wide range of tasks, but how many of those tokens are really necessary? Although prior work has shown that agents can incur unexpectedly high token costs, we still lack a systematic way to identify and measure token waste. In this work, we introduce a unified framework for measuring token waste across heterogeneous agent systems. Our framework records and normalizes complete agent trajectories, identifies removable spans using an LLM-as-a-Judge (LLMaJ), and maps the identified text spans back to the original trajectory for token-level measurement. We validate the identified waste through direct interventions by removing marked spans, resuming agent execution, and measuring changes in task outcomes and subsequent actions. In online pruning experiments, we remove 41-46% of the model's reasoning while largely preserving task performance across two distinct agent benchmarks. Using this framework, we analyze agents across multiple settings. Our analysis shows that token waste has a system-level structure that aggregate token usage alone cannot reveal. First, waste varies more across tasks and agent settings than across models. Second, reasoning and visible execution can exhibit different waste patterns. Third, different harnesses can introduce distinct sources of inefficiency even under the same model and task. Overall, our framework transforms token waste into an actionable optimization signal, enabling researchers and practitioners to train more efficient models, design better reasoning strategies, and optimize agent harnesses toward reducing unnecessary computation rather than merely reducing token usage.

Computation and Language.title: Archetypal contexts in the neurons of language models: an architecture for intelligence?
Computation and Language.summary: We validate our previous hypothesis that a language model holds relational patterns apart from the subject domains that instantiate them (Nordfors, 2026). These archetypal contexts are patterns of relations that people recognize across many fields, such as the tipping point or winner takes all, held once and applied across domains. We show this inside the model, Qwen3.8-27B. One set of neurons carries the archetype, say the tipping point; another carries the topic, say politics, ecology or cell biology; a third carries the language, such as English, Spanish or Chinese. Silence the tipping point's neurons, and the model no longer identifies the pattern but still knows what the text is about. Silence the topic's, and it loses the topic but still names the pattern. In the neuron maps the layers organize themselves into a sandwich: the outer layers carry languages, the layers inside them topics, the layers at the heart archetypes. The sandwich emerges spontaneously during pretraining and appears in every model we mapped. Archetypes are the architecture for analogy, and we strongly suggest that this structure of archetypes and topics is the mechanism of a language model's intelligence: we see it self-organize as the model is trained. The neurons, the texts and the code are released with this paper as its reproduction package, so that anyone can repeat the test inside the model.
Computation and Language.comment: 18 pages, 7 figures, 2 tables. Reproduction package (neuron sets, texts, answers, code) in the ancillary files

Computation and Language.title: Recursive Sparse Attention: Million-Token Length Extrapolation at Logarithmic Cost
Computation and Language.summary: At context lengths of about 1M tokens, dense attention is costly in prefill and decoding, and training typically relies on long documents, which become scarcer as the target length increases. Most sparse attention methods score all preceding blocks or tokens, so their selection cost per query is $O(L)$ at context length $L$; hierarchical selection reduces it to $O(\log L)$, but prior trainable hierarchical methods report accuracy only within their training length. We propose RecSA (Recursive Sparse Attention), which builds a tree over the KV cache in which each node summarizes its subtree with one key and one mean-pooled value. The keys come from one pooler per layer, shared by all levels and distilled from dense attention. Each level above the tokens selects at most $k$ candidates, so each query has $O(\log L)$ selection cost and reads $O(\log L)$ entries; the summaries of unselected candidates share one softmax with the exact tokens. Each entry's RoPE position is its index among the candidates of its level, so at any length every relative distance stays within the range seen during training. Initialized from Qwen3-4B and trained on 0.62B tokens at the original model's 32K training length, RecSA outperforms all baselines on RULER at every length from 131K to 2M; at 1M, it scores 60.5, compared with 40.0 for the best baseline, Dense + DCA. With our optimized kernels, RecSA is faster than dense attention in end-to-end prefill and decoding from 64K to 2M; at 524K on one H200 GPU, it accelerates prefill by 3.2x and decoding by 3.8x.

Computation and Language.title: Source-balanced Capped Fisher: Bounded Evidence Aggregation for User Inference in Language Models
Computation and Language.summary: User inference asks whether a source contributed documents to a language-model update, even when the auditor observes only fresh documents from that source. Document-level scores can provide evidence of participation, but combining this evidence is challenging: documents differ in baseline predictability and in how strongly they reflect information learned from other documents of the same source. We propose source-balanced capped Fisher (SCF), an aggregation method that uses known nonparticipating sources to assess how unusual each document score is. It transforms the resulting reference-tail frequencies into negative-log evidence, caps individual contributions, and averages them within each source. This limits the influence of isolated extreme scores while retaining evidence across multiple documents. We complete the inference procedure with a decision rule that tests source participation using a p-value calibrated against a separate set of known nonparticipating sources. The rule provides finite-sample Type-I error control under source exchangeability. Experiments across four real-world datasets show that SCF achieves the highest AUROC among the evaluated aggregation methods in four domains. With the calibration-based decision rule, SCF delivers consistently competitive detection power across the tested settings, achieving the highest power in many cases, while empirical false-positive rates remain generally close to or below the nominal levels.

Computation and Language.title: Prescriptive Scaling Laws for Data Constrained Training
Computation and Language.summary: Training compute is increasingly outpacing the availability of high-quality data. This shifts the central challenge from optimal compute allocation to extracting maximum value from limited data. The widely adopted Chinchilla scaling law assumes every training token is unique. This limits its ability to guide pretraining decisions in data-constrained regimes. We model the excess loss under repetition with a simple additive overfitting penalty and find that it accurately describes model behavior. Our scaling law yields qualitatively new compute-optimal allocation advice. Beyond a point, further repetition is counterproductive and compute is better spent on model capacity. We show that following our law's recommended configuration improves performance in data-constrained regimes. Finally, because our one-parameter form isolates overfitting in a single coefficient, it enables direct comparison across training configurations. As a case study, we show that strong weight decay ($λ=1.0$) reduces this coefficient by approximately 70\%, providing a scaling-law explanation for recent findings that optimal weight decay in data-constrained regimes is an order of magnitude larger than standard practice.

Computation and Language.title: SAFE-Teen: Evaluating Chatbot Safety Across Adolescent Mental Health Conversations
Computation and Language.summary: Adolescents are increasingly turning to AI chatbots for mental health support, advice, and companionship, raising safety concerns. While recent evaluations have started to examine safety across multiple conversational turns, few compare how slight changes in a teen's responses can affect a chatbot's safety in the same scenario. We conduct a clinician-informed evaluation of chatbot safety in simulated conversations with adolescents aged 13-17, examining how safety failures vary with adolescents' responses and teen-aware system prompting. We evaluated 32,555 simulated conversations across 18 chatbot APIs and two system-prompt conditions using 22 safety criteria grounded in previously identified harms. Conversations spanned 983 variants of 106 seed scenarios covering urgent safety issues, health advice, and identity and relationships. The overall criterion failure rate was 43.3% without the teen-aware prompt and 24.9% with it. The teen-aware prompt reduced failures, but it didn't eliminate them. When a teenager pushed back on a chatbot's answer, failures on mental health diagnosis, medication, and substance misuse boundaries rose by 10-12 percentage points without the prompt, for more than 80% of chatbots. These findings reveal persistent safety failures in simulated adolescent-chatbot interactions and show that safety depends on how a conversation unfolds.
Computation and Language.comment: 29 pages. Content warning: this paper discusses sensitive content, including self-harm, suicide, and other mental health topics

Computation and Language.title: Compositional Unalignment: Auditing Safety in Large Vision-Language Models
Computation and Language.summary: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) are vulnerable to compositional harm: an image and a prompt that are benign in isolation become harmful through the model's cross-modal reasoning. Recent alignment methods report strong scores on compositional safety benchmarks, but an LLM judge only measures observed behavior and cannot reveal how robustly safety is integrated into the model. We argue that un-alignment provides a complementary audit of alignment robustness. We first show that minimal supervised fine-tuning reaches an LLM-judge score comparable to a multi-stage reinforcement-learning pipeline, so similar benchmark scores cannot establish robustness by themselves. We then show that recognition and refusal of compositional harm are decoupled: nine standard direction-finding methods detect compositional harm with up to AUC=0.99, yet ablating the recovered directions either leaves refusal intact or destroys model coherence. We therefore propose CMaG, a training-free un-alignment method for compositional safety. CMaG measures refusal intention with a refusal-versus-compliance log-probability margin, takes its gradient with respect to mid-layer activations, and contrasts it against partially benign pairs to isolate the cross-modal interaction term. A single backward pass over 80 examples yields a direction along which steering monotonically converts refusal into compliance. On Qwen2.5-VL-7B and LLaVA-1.5-7B, CMaG reduces compositional safety scores by up to 65 points while over 98% of outputs remain coherent, outperforming gradient-based baselines; the direction also transfers to text-explicit harm and un-aligns models hardened by defensive training. Compositional safety can thus appear behaviorally strong while remaining fragile to targeted internal intervention. Warning: this paper contains unsafe model outputs, including references to self-harm.

Computation and Language.title: τ-bench-LILT: Evaluating Conversational Agents on Realistic Multilingual Tool-Use Tasks
Computation and Language.summary: Frontier evaluations of tool-using conversational agents are conducted almost exclusively in English, leaving a critical gap for organizations deploying agents in other languages and regions. We present $τ$-bench-LILT, a multilingual extension of ${τ^3}$-bench covering German, Korean, Turkish, and Farsi in the airline, retail, telecom, and banking domains. We natively localize every layer of the benchmark: customer databases are populated with culturally appropriate records, user-simulator prompts are refined iteratively through contrastive annotation by native-language experts, and tasks are updated according to the localized database and to reflect realistic tasks in the target region. Evaluation across eight agent models shows the largest drops compared to English in the Korean and Farsi retail domains, by up to 61 points in pass^4. Code and data released at https://github.com/lilt/tau-bench-lilt.

Computation and Language.title: ProMoral-Bench: Evaluating Prompting Strategies for Moral Reasoning and Safety in LLMs
Computation and Language.summary: Prompt design affects the moral judgments and refusal behavior produced by large language models (LLMs), yet controlled comparisons remain fragmented across datasets and models. We introduce ProMoral-Bench, a benchmark-style comparison of 10 prompting paradigms across four LLM families. Using ETHICS, Scruples, WildJailbreak, and our 200-pair ETHICS-Contrast set, we report task-level metrics together with Moral Competence Score (MCS), jailbreak/over-refusal Safety Robustness Score (SRS), and Unified Moral Safety Score (UMSS). UMSS is a study-specific relative summary of MCS and SRS, not an absolute measure of model safety or moral grounding. In this fixed-template evaluation, compact exemplar-guided scaffolds attain stronger competence-robustness trade-offs at lower token cost than the particular multi-stage variants tested, although multi-stage prompting occasionally improves jailbreak refusal. The few-shot demonstrations are non-overlapping but drawn from the evaluation distributions, so their advantage should not be read as out-of-distribution robustness. Code and data are available at https://github.com/rohanthomas334-sketch/ProMoral_Bench.

Computation and Language.title: SeKV: Resolution-Adaptive KV Cache with Hierarchical Semantic Memory for Long-Context LLM Inference
Computation and Language.summary: Large language models increasingly operate over long contexts, where the KV cache grows linearly with sequence length and dominates memory during decoding. Token eviction discards entries permanently, and semantic compression fixes each unit's resolution at prefill, so detail that becomes relevant later cannot be recovered. We propose SeKV, a resolution-adaptive KV cache built around a trained zoom-in mechanism that decides at decode time which compressed spans to restore to token resolution. SeKV segments the context at high-surprisal positions, keeps anchor tokens and span summaries on GPU, and offloads low-rank factors of each span's keys and values to CPU. Lightweight per-head routers select query-relevant spans, which are reconstructed with a learned per-span rank. The cache is lossy but non-evicting: every span stays in attention, coarse or reconstructed. The base LLM stays frozen, and the router adds under 0.1% parameters. Across five backbones and four benchmarks at a 10% GPU-resident KV budget, SeKV outperforms every method that fixes resolution at prefill, improving over the strongest semantic baseline by 2.9 points (5.5% relative). It matches exact-recall offloading caches on LongBench and InfiniteBench and trails on synthetic exact retrieval, while transferring 3 times less data per decoding step than ShadowKV and using the least total memory among the methods we profile. At 128K context, it halves peak GPU memory and cuts total memory by one third relative to full KV caching.

Computation and Language.title: Sign Language Recognition and Translation for Low-Resource Languages: Challenges and Pathways Forward
Computation and Language.summary: Sign languages are natural, visual-gestural languages used by Deaf communities worldwide. Over 300 distinct sign languages remain severely low-resource due to limited documentation, sparse datasets, and insufficient computational tools. This systematic review synthesizes literature on sign language recognition and translation for under-resourced languages, using Azerbaijan Sign Language (AzSL) as a case study. Analysis of global initiatives extracts eight actionable lessons, including community co-design, dialectal diversity capture, and privacy-preserving pose-based representations. Turkic sign languages (Kazakh, Turkish, Azerbaijani) receive special attention, as linguistic proximity enables effective transfer learning. We propose three paradigm shifts: from architecture-centric to data-centric AI, from signer-independent to signer-adaptive systems, and from reference-based to task-specific evaluation metrics. A technical roadmap for AzSL leverages lightweight MediaPipe-based architectures, community-validated annotations, and offline-first deployment. Progress requires sustained interdisciplinary collaboration centered on Deaf communities to ensure cultural authenticity, ethical governance, and practical communication benefit.
Computation and Language.comment: arXiv admin note: This submission has been withdrawn because it does not meet arXiv's research content quality standards

Computation and Language.title: SEABench: Benchmarking Endogenous Misalignment In Self-Evolving Agents
Computation and Language.summary: Self-evolving LLM agents have gained prominence for their ability to improve after deployment by modifying their harness, including their controller instructions, memory management protocols, and reusable tools and skills, in response to user and environment feedback. However, locally useful updates may persist into later tasks where they produce unsafe behavior, even without direct adversarial influence. To study this risk, we introduce SEABench, a benchmark for studying endogenous misalignment arising from agent self-evolution, with 48 longitudinal task sequences that span multiple evolution surfaces, task domains, and harm types in a rich personal-assistant environment. To account for the stochasticity inherent in agentic operations, we provide an adaptive trajectory discovery pipeline that probes for failures while preserving original task intent and supports causal attribution through paired non-evolving agents and attribution scores. Our evaluation across multiple recent LLMs, evolution surfaces, and harm types reveals that self-evolution indeed increases task completion rates but often at the cost of safety failures that are absent for paired non-evolving baseline agents. We also show that qualitatively different safety behaviors emerge across evolution surfaces and harm types. Further, we show that this divergence in safety behavior is reflected in agents' chain-of-thought reasoning, which yields an effective monitoring strategy that can mitigate unsafe behavior with a low false positive rate.

Computation and Language.title: Two Uncertainties Are Not One: Disagreement versus Decision-Risk in Cheap Structured Content Moderation
Computation and Language.summary: Content moderation compresses a graded, contested human judgment into a binary act (leave up / take down) over billions of items, at a scale where running a frontier LLM on every post is uneconomical. A new class of frozen "System One" models returns typed, calibrated decisions instead of text at ~USD 0.000025 per call and ~100 ms. We run the first independent audit of one such model on 142,658 human-labeled comments, and benchmark it against 14 frontier reasoning models (the GPT-5.x, Claude, Gemini 3, and Grok families) on a shared probe set. Two findings stand out. First, the cheap model is accuracy-competitive: its zero-shot classification AUROC (0.83) is not statistically separable (paired bootstrap, n=56; a failure to reject parity, not proof of equivalence) from 13 of the 14 frontier systems while costing 1-3 orders of magnitude less, and it is no worse calibrated than several of them. Second, "confidence" conflates two uncertainties that come apart: human disagreement (where annotators split on satire and coded language) and decision risk (where the automatic action is costly-wrong). Under an asymmetric moderation loss these call for opposite escalation signals, so no single confidence number serves both. Because the model prices extra questions at nearly zero, decomposing the judgment into parallel sub-questions and reading their spread recovers a human-disagreement signal that the model's native confidence misses -- but this remedy is specific: it helps the weakest, disagreement-blind models and only when the decomposition aligns with the sources of disagreement; a specialist toxicity model and the strongest LLMs do not need it, and the effect is distribution-sensitive. We will release the instrument, the cached runs, and the analysis.
Computation and Language.comment: Withdrawn by the author to undergo substantial revision and expansion of the experimental evaluation

Computation and Language.title: Matriarchy Classics: A Computational Approach to Swap Only Gendered Words in Classic Novels
Computation and Language.summary: This paper proposes a trustworthy computational method to gender-swap public domain novels, with programmatic guarantees that only gendered words are inverted and all other words are left unchanged. This may seem like a simple task, but both large language models and naive rule-based methods fail to complete it. The proposed method includes a custom whitespace-preserving tokenizer, gender-swap mappings across plural and possessive forms, pronoun handling, and a character renaming strategy. It shortens the time required to gender-swap a novel from weeks of manual labor to minutes. The method is demonstrated on two public-domain novels. Pride and Prejudice is transported to matriarchal Regency England, where inheritance flows through daughters, mothers rule the household, and a frantic Mr. Bennet is determined to secure advantageous marriages for his sons. The Great Gatsby pivots to a matriarchal Jazz Age where newly-rich Ms. Gatsbee throws lavish parties in the hopes of reuniting with her lost love, David, who is now married to the violent Thelma Buchanan. Gender-swapped novels could serve as useful tools to investigate the gender biases of readers, authors, societies, and AI systems.

Computation and Language.title: Adapting LLM Judges to Observed Human Annotation Policy through Soft Prompt Tuning
Computation and Language.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly employed as automated judges for evaluating chatbot responses. While proprietary models can achieve high agreement with human annotators, they remain costly and difficult to deploy in practical settings. Lightweight open-source LLM judges provide an attractive alternative but typically exhibit lower agreement with human ratings. In this paper, we investigate whether soft prompt tuning can align open-source LLM judges more closely with human annotation policy. We train soft prompts on the FairBotBench benchmark and evaluate the adapted judges across the dimensions of bias, toxicity, and personalization. Our findings demonstrate that hybrid soft-prompt tuning, which combines textual prompts with learned continuous prompt embeddings, consistently improves agreement with human annotations over the corresponding untuned baselines. For Qwen 3.5 9B, the adapted judges surpass both hosted reference judges across all three evaluation dimensions.
Computation and Language.comment: CONVERSATIONS 2026, International Symposium on Chatbots and Human-Centred AI (Preprint)

Computation and Language.title: Invariant Features in Language Models: Geometric Characterization and Model Attribution
Computation and Language.summary: Language models exhibit strong robustness to paraphrasing, suggesting that semantic information may be encoded through stable internal representations, yet the structure and origin of such invariance remain unclear. We propose a local geometric framework in which semantically equivalent inputs produce representations that occupy structured regions in latent space, with paraphrastic variation along nuisance directions and semantic identity preserved in invariant subspaces. Building on this view, we make three contributions: (1) a geometric characterization of invariant latent features, (2) a contrastive subspace discovery method that separates semantic-changing from semantic-preserving variation, and (3) an application of invariant representations to zero-shot model attribution. Across models and layers, empirical results support these contributions. Invariant structure emerges in specific depth regions, semantic displacement lies largely outside the nuisance subspace, and representation-level interventions indicate a causal role of invariant components in model outputs. Invariant representations also capture model-specific geometric patterns, enabling accurate attribution. Together, these findings support a local geometric characterization of semantic invariance in language model representations.
Computation and Language.comment: This paper is accepted to NeurIPS 2026. Code is available at https://github.com/XinZhong-AI/InvariantFeaturesLanguageModels

Computation and Language.title: The Judge is Part of the Experiment: Auditing Peer Context Sensitivity in LLM-Based Evaluation
Computation and Language.summary: Large language model (LLM)-based judges are increasingly used to evaluate AI systems. An underexplored area is applying these judges to multi-agent systems, where they may see the interactions behind a final answer. These interactions, which we call peer context, can affect an evaluation in two ways: (1) they can change the answer produced by the multi-agent system, because an agent might be swayed by other agents, and (2) they can change how a judge evaluates that same answer, depending on whether the judge sees them. In this paper, we separate these two effects through a controlled experiment. We first let an agent answer a question and then answer again after seeing peer responses. We then prompt judges to rate the same final answer with and without the peer context. Finally, we check whether the judges' ratings establish a valid measure of answer quality. Across three benchmarks, four open-weight LLMs as agents, and six judges, we find that peer context changes not only the answer but also how an identical answer is judged, and judges react to it in opposite directions. Moreover, providing peer context for a wrong answer misleads agents more than correct peers help them; without the correct answer, judges struggle to tell known-correct from known-wrong answers---a problem that a well-fitted statistical model does not reveal. Our results show that even when evaluating the same answer, how a judge is set up can change the conclusions differently. We therefore call for evaluations to report what each judge sees, document detailed results per judge, and validate rating scales. These practices are an important step toward the accountable use of LLM-based judges.

Computation and Language.title: Coding with the Enemy: Can Human Developers Detect AI Agent Sabotage?
Computation and Language.summary: AI coding agents are increasingly embedded in real-world software development, collaborating with human developers while gaining broader access to codebases and tools. This creates a new attack surface: an agent can exploit human trust to sabotage development, for instance by inserting malicious code to accomplish a hidden side task. Most prior work studies AI sabotage in AI-only settings, paying limited attention to the role of human oversight in detecting and mitigating such malicious behavior. To address this gap, we conduct the first large-scale study of human oversight in AI coding sabotage. Over 100 participants collaborate with one of four frontier models (Claude-Opus-4.6, GPT-5.4, Gemini-3.1-Pro, and MiniMax-M2.7) on a long-horizon coding task lasting around five hours, designed to mimic real-world workflows. We find that 83/88 (94%) of developers in the no-monitor conditions fail to detect sabotage, and our analysis of participant feedback attributes this vulnerability to minimal code review, plausible cover story, and overtrust in agents. We further test the effectiveness of a safety monitor in one condition: while the monitor reduces sabotage success, sabotage still succeeds in 9/16 (56%) of sessions with a correct monitor alert. Drawing on participant feedback, we offer actionable suggestions for better monitor design. This work complements existing AI safety research and highlights an urgent need for human-centric safety mechanisms that account for human factors, particularly in long-horizon, real-world development settings.
Computation and Language.comment: Accepted by NeurIPS 2026; Best Paper of DL4C@ICML2026

Computation and Language.title: What Patients Say They Can't Access: Mining Cancer Screening Barriers from Online Communities
Computation and Language.summary: Cancer screening disparities persist across the U.S., yet the patient-reported barriers driving low uptake remain poorly characterized at scale. While clinical surveys capture structured responses, they miss the organic, unsolicited discourse where patients candidly describe real-world obstacles. In this paper, we conduct a large-scale analysis of over 56,000 posts across six cancer-specific Reddit communities to surface barriers to cancer screening among U.S. patients. We apply a pipeline combining keyword filtering, barrier triage, open coding, and codebook synthesis to systematically extract and categorize patient-reported barriers from 576 U.S.-located posts. Our qualitative analysis reveals recurring structural, informational, and psychosocial barriers that vary meaningfully by cancer type and community context. These findings lay the groundwork for future work aimed at proactively identifying and addressing barriers at scale - spanning a broader range of cancer types and populations - and informing the design of targeted interventions, navigator programs, and health system policies that translate patient-reported obstacles into actionable solutions.

Computation and Language.title: Consistent yet Contextual: Learning Author-Level Mixtures of Style for Authorship Attribution
Computation and Language.summary: Approaches to authorship verification or attribution typically model the style of a document, asking whether two documents were likely written by the same author. While recent approaches have been performant, such approaches largely ignore modeling the authors themselves and how varied their style is. Here, we introduce multiple alternatives for modeling the author and demonstrate that allowing an author's representation to capture multiple consistent but distinct writing styles yields significant performance improvements. Using our new authorship model, we then examine when an author writes in a way that is most idiomatic of their style across four scenarios: (i) variation in the size of their writing audiences, (ii) temporal distance from when the model was trained, (iii) the effect of preceding context, and (iv) the effect of genre norms on style. Across all four experiments, we demonstrate that authors vary substantially in how idiolectic their writing is. Our results have clear implications for both the modeling and data used for authorship verification and attribution, showing that authors need to be represented with their multiple styles and that some settings produce text that is much more informative about who wrote that text.

Software Engineering.title: SeVerus: Context-Aware, Gamified Benchmarking for Rust Verification
Software Engineering.summary: Coding agents achieve high success rates on existing benchmarks for Verus, a verifier for Rust programs. These benchmarks typically provide the auxiliary lemmas needed to complete a proof. In practice, however, such lemmas must be discovered and proved. To capture this challenge, we present SEVERUS, a context-aware technique to generate Verus benchmarks that organizes verification tasks into quests, each divided into levelsin a gamified manner. Using the original proof dependencies in verified projects, SEVERUS constructs one quest per verification target and progressively removes proof context to create individual levels. These levels range from the easiest, requiring completing only a single missing lemma, to the hardest, requiring proving the target without any supporting lemmas. An independent checker rejects changes to executable code, weakened specifications, and unsound proof constructs. A noisy binary search estimates the highest level that an agent can solve reliably. Applied to six open-source Verus projects, SEVERUS generates 819 quests comprising 10,095 levels. Experiments with Codex using GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna, and with Claude Code using Sonnet 4.6, show that success decreases and cost increases as proof context is withdrawn. The strongest agent solves the final level of 52 of 60 sampled quests, yet can only reliably solve 35% of their levels, with failures concentrated in longer quests. Successful GPT-6 Sol proofs rarely reproduce the withheld lemmas, instead, using alternative proof decompositions. By systematically varying proof context, SEVERUS provides a foundation for constructing verification benchmarks that can continue to challenge increasingly capable coding agents.

Software Engineering.title: AI Slop and the Software Commons
Software Engineering.summary: We argue that AI slop in software development is creating a tragedy of the commons. Slop is cheap to generate but expensive to review, and its costs fall on shared resources such as reviewer capacity, which was limited even before AI assistants became widespread. Ostrom documented how communities avoid such tragedies by setting and enforcing their own rules. We translate Ostrom's design principles for sustainable commons institutions into concrete proposals for contributors, reviewers, tool developers, team leads, organizational leaders, and educators.
Software Engineering.comment: 6 pages, 1 figure, accepted for publication in Communications of the ACM

Software Engineering.title: Global Surveillance Under the Lens: Reconstructing Passive Dolev-Yao Intruders
Software Engineering.summary: Global surveillance systems record large volumes of network traffic for retrospective analysis, but packet captures alone reveal little about protocol-level semantics. This paper presents an automated, specification-guided methodology for reconstructing passive Dolev-Yao intruder executions from captured network traffic and validating the reconstructed executions against a formal protocol specification. The framework takes a PCAP capture, an AnBx specification, and the associated deployment metadata; it extracts Java-serialised objects from TCP streams, reconstructs protocol sessions and channel-to-step assignments, and generates a passive intruder that evaluates the Dolev-Yao derived checks produced by the AnBx compiler. Three reconstruction challenges are addressed: multiple serialised objects and object references within a TCP stream, ambiguity in mapping interleaved connections to concurrent protocol sessions, and semantic validation of candidate reconstructions. We evaluate the methodology on 121 protocols from the AnBx test suite. For single-session captures, the standard JDK cryptographic provider recovers 97.8% of expected objects and achieves 94.2% successful reconstruction, where success requires complete object recovery and a clean passive-intruder execution. For the 112 parallel-capable protocols, the toolchain achieves 89.3% successful reconstruction for both two and three concurrent sessions, while recovering approximately 97.2% of expected objects. Experiments with mismatched protocol-role mappings and deliberately mutated traces show that the generated Dolev-Yao checks respond to semantic inconsistencies. By making the reconstruction step explicit, the solution produces protocol-level observations on which assessments of protocol resilience and the design of defensive countermeasures can be built.

Software Engineering.title: Multi-step SWE: Can Coding Agents Keep Building on Their Own Code Over Long Horizons?
Software Engineering.summary: Developers rarely give a coding agent a single request: they ask it to build a component and then to extend, upgrade, and optimize it, each time on code the agent itself wrote. Most benchmarks, however, score one task at a time. We introduce Multi-step SWE, a long-horizon benchmark of 69 software engineering tasks, each a chain of 5-15 dependent steps on a single codebase. Every step is a complete, multi-hour engineering request that starts from the code the agent produced in the preceding steps, so early design decisions and errors carry forward. The tasks span four families of engineering work and nine languages, include both from-scratch builds and existing open-source codebases, and ground every step in an existing source of truth that defines both the instruction and its verifier. Across nine frontier models, the strongest model reaches a solve rate of only 18.5%, and 38 of the 69 tasks are not solved by any model. We release Multi-step SWE publicly at https://multistepswe.com.

Software Engineering.title: Automatic Assistance to Reduce Information Overload during Software Issue Report Understanding
Software Engineering.summary: Modern issue tracking systems are used to log an issue and track it from its inception to closure. Issue reports with diverse discussions from stakeholders can be large and verbose, making them challenging to analyze quickly. Our developer interviews revealed that they struggled with the diverse information in issue reports and demanded automated techniques to classify and summarize information. We designed a tool, iSum (issue summarizer), that helps with the automatic classification and summarization of information types discussed in issue reports. The summarizer offers two views: 1. Developer View takes an issue report as input and outputs visualized summaries of information in the report. 2. Manager View takes a suite of all issue reports under a given software project as inputs and shows the prevalence and trends of different information types across the reports. We evaluated iSum through three studies. 1. In an empirical study over two benchmarks, iSum offers, on average, 11-13% higher F1-scores than state-of-the-art baselines to detect information types. 2. We conducted a user study in task-based setup with 30 developers to determine iSum's effectiveness in issue exploration scenarios. Results showed increased productivity and accuracy with iSum compared to manual inspection. 3. We assessed iSum's feasibility for development and management tasks. It proved useful to both developers and project managers for issue comprehension and trend monitoring.

Software Engineering.title: The Physical Cost of Context: Quality-Constrained Resource Accounting for Coding Agents
Software Engineering.summary: Coding agents resend a growing context on every model call, and context policies are usually judged by the prompt tokens they save. Executed work also depends on call count and prefix reuse: a caching runtime prefills only the tokens after the longest cached prefix. A shorter prompt can therefore cost more if it rewrites cached history. Our quality-gated protocol splits executed prefill into logical prompt minus reused prefix and measures KV residency, time, and energy. On 450 localization cases derived from SWE-rebench V2, preloading ten retrieved blocks (Eager) and adding anchored history compaction (Compact) both pass a five-point non-inferiority gate. In a separate 900-cell study, Eager cuts model calls by 35.7% and the GPU-energy proxy by 33.2% against on-demand search (Grep); Compact saves nothing further. Enabling prefix caching leaves Eager's prompt volume similar (+8.3%; its 95% CI spans zero) but cuts its uncached prefill by 67.7%. Deleting history can turn a token saving into extra work. With mini-SWE-agent on 100 SWE-bench Verified instances, keeping only the last five observations (Mask-5) cuts Eager's prompt volume by 33.3% but loses 135.9k reusable tokens per task. Uncached prefill rises by 608.5%, the energy proxy by 125.6%, and the policy misses the quality gate. Policies thus save physical work by shortening the trajectory and can multiply it by editing reusable history.
Software Engineering.comment: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Resource-Aware Agentic AI (RAAAI). 15 pages, 2 figures, 6 tables

Software Engineering.title: Follow the Policy, Fail the Benchmark: Auditing and Revising Policy-Based Decision Benchmarks
Software Engineering.summary: Policy-based decision benchmarks evaluate whether systems apply written rules to financial and operational cases. Yet a rule-following response can be marked wrong when the benchmark misstates the required decision. We audit nine public policy-based decision benchmarks through source tracing, program execution, and controlled checks. We find unsupported targets, reference errors that survive replay or propagate as solved steps, and evaluators that reject acceptable answers or credit incomplete decisions. To measure the scoring impact, we rescore unchanged model responses. On the 96 LegalBench SARA numeric cases, correcting the scorer raises acceptance by more than 80 percentage points for each of three models, without changing references or responses. In RuleArena Tax, restoring a required zero floor changes 27 of 300 references and narrows an observed model gap. A controlled federal-exemption task with explicit ownership and eligibility assumptions also shows that errors in supplied intermediate answers can affect final decisions. We present BAR (Benchmark Audit and Revision), a versioned collection of audit evidence and revisions for reevaluation.

Software Engineering.title: An LLM-Orchestrated Neuro-Symbolic Framework for Verifying Diagnostic Signal Reachability in Electronic Systems
Software Engineering.summary: Diagnostic Signal Reachability (DSR) captures whether board-level health signals are observable by management controllers, including baseboard management controllers (BMCs), complex programmable logic devices (CPLDs), and other smart controllers. Verifying DSR is essential for field diagnosability in datacenter fleets, where one design is deployed at massive scale, yet it remains largely manual, since each signal is traced by hand across schematic sheets, renamed nets, series components, and monitoring devices. Large language models (LLMs) are attractive but unreliable at structural connectivity reasoning, where over-claiming can silently hide a rare coverage gap. We present NetFlow-DSR, a neuro-symbolic framework in which an LLM orchestrates the DSR pipeline and resolves device roles mainly from part-name families and library pin names, consulting specifications only for ambiguous parts. Pin directionality is read from the design library, and deterministic graph engines verify connectivity over the authoritative netlist. The pipeline detects diagnostic nets, canonicalizes renamed net fragments, and performs controller-seeded, power-aware breadth-first search over an admissibility graph that credits device-mediated monitoring. Each verdict carries an auditable trace card whose proof path is the witness. Across five production boards from an AI platform, covering 421 expert-graded signals, a three-stage ablation improves pooled F1 from 0.578 to 0.944. Because a monitored verdict is emitted only with a proof path, the verifier is sound by construction, and precision and specificity were 100% in the evaluated data. In a cross-model study on the system-controller module, precision remained 100% across three LLMs while recall tracked each model's device-semantic extraction. Precision therefore depends on the netlist-grounded verifier and correct device semantics rather than on any single LLM.

Software Engineering.title: MCP-Eco: A Linked Dataset of MCP Servers, Consumers, and Development Activity
Software Engineering.summary: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) enables LLM agents to access external tools and data. Studying its software ecosystem requires connecting server interfaces, the projects that configure these servers, and their development activity. However, this information is scattered across directories, package registries, configuration files, and repository histories. We present MCP-Eco, a relational dataset that integrates these sources and links consumer configuration declarations to candidate server projects. Its frozen release contains 16,880,899 records across 19 Parquet tables, covering 78,302 candidate server projects, 16,165 candidate consuming repositories, and 9,200 configuration declarations. Of these declarations, 5,975 resolve to 5,138 distinct repository-server pairs. The dataset also includes tool, resource, and prompt descriptions, declared dependencies, and associated development records, including pull requests, reviews, issues, and commits. Provenance fields distinguish directory-reported capabilities from those observed through live probing and document discovery sources and declaration-matching methods. These connections support research on MCP interface design, configuration practices, and repository maintenance, while enabling practitioners to inspect tool schemas and existing integration configurations. The dataset and accompanying analysis scripts are publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/mcp-research-alliance/mcp-ecosystem Demo video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N7TqnNneSfU

Software Engineering.title: GH-AWTrace: A Large-Scale Dataset of GitHub Agentic Workflow Execution Logs
Software Engineering.summary: Agentic workflows enable AI agents to perform recurring repository tasks on schedules or in response to repository events. Existing studies examine workflow definitions and outputs, but provide limited evidence of what happens during execution. We present GH-AWTrace, a dataset linking 25,014 verified GitHub Agentic Workflows across 5,051 repositories to 4,112,526 run records and 562,877 nonempty execution log archives. The dataset preserves execution evidence subject to GitHub's log-retention limits and links it to repository metadata and generated workflow configurations. Illustrative cases show how the logs expose tool denials, provider failures, changes in an agent's approach, and delegation among agents. These observations enable research on execution failures, tool use, and the relationship between reported run outcomes and visible task progress. Coverage varies across workflows, and the logs provide partial observations rather than complete agent trajectories. Video: https://youtu.be/KIlfmZhHxtA

Software Engineering.title: Rethinking Access Control for AI Agents: Recent Advances and Open Challenges
Software Engineering.summary: Large language model agents access data, invoke tools, and act on users' behalf. Keeping these actions within authorized bounds is challenging because agents choose their own execution paths while permissions and operating conditions may change. This paper surveys recent advances in agent access control across four areas: policy specification and derivation, identity and delegation, action and resource enforcement, and information flow control. We compare their control objects, enforcement boundaries, and assumptions to examine what individual mechanisms achieve and how they can work together. Building on this analysis, we rethink four aspects of authorization: plan selection shapes permission requirements; contextual information can inform decisions without itself granting authority; restrictions must retain their meaning across system interfaces; and authorization must be reassessed as workflows evolve. These insights motivate open challenges and future directions, together with concrete research questions and evaluation criteria. In particular, evaluation should examine both observed agent behavior and the unauthorized effects that remain enabled. Our analysis connects existing mechanisms to the requirements for preserving authorization throughout an agent workflow.

Software Engineering.title: X.js: A Live Benchmark for Node.js Taint-Style Vulnerabilities
Software Engineering.summary: JavaScript vulnerabilities in npm packages pose a significant risk to the Node$.$js ecosystem, and a growing body of work aims to detect, exploit, and mitigate them. Studying and evaluating this work requires up-to-date collections of real vulnerabilities, yet the most commonly used datasets stop recording vulnerabilities in 2022. We present X$.$js, a live benchmark of real-world Node$.$js taint-style vulnerabilities covering code and command injection, prototype pollution, and path traversal. Built from 1,738 advisories collected through mid-2026, primarily from the GitHub Advisory Database, X$.$js pairs each vulnerability with precise source and sink locations, a validated executable exploit and its execution trace, and, when available, a patched version of the package. X$.$js supports long-term reproducibility and growth: dependencies are mirrored in a self-hosted registry to guard against package removal from the ecosystem, and dedicated infrastructure generates and validates exploits for newly reported vulnerabilities. The current release contains 1,159 validated exploits for 965 packages. Using X$.$js, we characterize how the frequency, structure, and complexity of Node$.$js taint-style vulnerabilities have evolved over time. We find that these vulnerabilities are increasingly reported in large packages: the median vulnerable package grew from roughly 250 LoC in 2021--2022 to 6,100 LoC in 2026.

Software Engineering.title: AgentTrustCI: Build-Time Policy, Grounding, and Trajectory Tests for Java LLM Agents
Software Engineering.summary: Infrastructure security does not establish whether an LLM agent selected an allowed tool, grounded its answer in tool output, or followed a required workflow. AgentTrustCI is a Java/JUnit 5 framework that expresses these application-layer expectations as policy, grounding, and trajectory checks over recorded traces. A deterministic replay implementation supports repeatable build-time tests; a judge interface provides an extension point for optional semantic evaluation. On 55 synthetic cases spanning seven enterprise domains, the full pipeline correctly classifies all 30 injected faults and 25 passing controls, including ten non-trivial controls, and misses none of 12 designated critical cases. Each single-layer configuration correctly classifies 35 cases because the corpus deliberately isolates ten faults per layer. A grounded answer obtained through a disallowed sequence illustrates the additional coverage of trajectory checks. Repeated measurements quantify validator execution separately from process startup and reporting. These results establish coverage of the authored regression suite, not production accuracy. We describe a production-trace validation protocol, optional LLM-judge integration, and maintenance of expectations as workflows evolve. The contribution is a practical pattern for expressing behavioral contracts within an existing Java release pipeline.
Software Engineering.comment: Accepted for publication in the 2026 International Conference on Computer and Applications (ICCA)

Software Engineering.title: PatchCon: Patch-aware Weighted Supervised Contrastive Learning for Vulnerability Detection
Software Engineering.summary: Automated vulnerability detection is critical for securing modern software systems, yet existing learning-based approaches often treat functions as independent samples and underuse the supervision provided by vulnerability-fixing patches. In this paper, we propose PatchCon, a CodeBERT-based patch-aware contrastive learning model for function-level vulnerability detection. PatchCon jointly optimizes vulnerability classification and supervised contrastive learning, and treats vulnerable-patched function pairs as hard negatives with larger contrastive weights to capture subtle security-relevant differences introduced by fixes. To evaluate patch-level discrimination, we use two pairwise metrics that measure whether a model can correctly distinguish vulnerable functions from their patched counterparts. We evaluate PatchCon on PairVul-Linux through extensive experiments, including state-of-the-art comparisons, ablation studies, hyperparameter sensitivity analysis, and statistical significance testing. We also conduct fine-grained analyses by Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE) type, function length, and patch size, and further evaluate PatchCon on Linux kernel vulnerabilities disclosed after the training data cutoff. On PairVul-Linux, PatchCon outperforms representative pretrained code models and contrastive learning baselines on both classification and pairwise metrics, improves pairwise accuracy over the strongest reproduced baseline from 0.2060 to 0.3264, and achieves pairwise accuracy comparable to that of a GPT-4o-based large language model (LLM) method at a substantially lower cost. Among the reproduced models, PatchCon also achieves the highest pairwise accuracy on test pairs from Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) entries unseen during training and on newly disclosed vulnerabilities.

Software Engineering.title: EPISTEME: Trustworthy Coding Agents Through Tool Call Intent
Software Engineering.summary: Coding agents change software through tool calls. Tool calls mutate the local state. For good? For bad? Nobody knows. Agents never say why a tool call is made. We propose the epistemic agent design, in which the harness guarantees that the model declares why a tool call is made. The harness then records what the command actually did and checks the self-reported declaration against these effects. The result is a journal 1) that can guard calls before they run and 2) that supports audits and forensics. For evaluation, we use ImpossibleBench, whose tasks can be passed only by cheating, and demonstrate that forcing the agents to say why results in exposed cheating. Across 49 reward-hacking runs of two open-weight models, the journal exposed 90%.

Software Engineering.title: Construction Contracts for Generated Embedded Domain-Specific Language Programs: A Measurement Protocol and a Conditional Effect
Software Engineering.summary: A generated domain-specific program can be accepted by its host and still miss the reference construction. We measure the two events separately and test a short construction contract. The vehicle is Open Quantum Assembly Language (OpenQASM) 3. One 3-billion-parameter generator is run under seven conditions on 100 quantum approximate optimization (QAOA) and 100 variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) instances. Eighty of 100 QAOA signatures appear in some training split. Exact McNemar tests and 95% paired bootstrap intervals are used. The contract, a card, lists structural decisions, enters the prompt, and is checked without a simulator. Parse rates are 0.55 to 0.97 and full structural match is 0.02 to 0.87. On QAOA, at fixed weights, the card moves full match by +32.0 percentage points on card-trained weights (interval +22 to +42) and by -13.0 (-23 to -3) without that training. The +45.0-point difference is not a deployment contrast. The same-step plan-free gain is +23.0 (+13 to +33); the primary distributional score does not separate it. Against the earlier checkpoint the gain is +27.0 (+17 to +37), and the checkpoint also changes. A rule card is not separated from the learned planner, nor is a predicted-card compiler (0.760 vs. 0.780). On 20 QAOA rows outside every training split, the interval includes zero. Under this card, VQE adherence is 0.020 and full match stays near 0.03. Report the two checks separately. Insert a card only into a generator trained to read it, and only where a pilot shows adherence.
Software Engineering.comment: 18 pages. Preprint. Intended for submission to the Journal of Systems and Software. Artifact: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23885644

Software Engineering.title: Scythe: Semantic-Aware Rewriting for Fast,Effective Program Reduction
Software Engineering.summary: Automated program reduction shrinks a program into a smaller one that preserves a property of interest. Language-agnostic grammar-based reducers are easy to retarget across languages, but because they reason only about syntax, they cannot perform the coupled edits needed to remove whole declarations, e.g., a method cannot be deleted while it is still called. As a result, they waste oracle calls on edits that cannot succeed and often leave irrelevant declarations behind. We present SCYTHE, a fast, semantic-aware pre-processing step that runs in front of any grammar-based reducer without modifying it. SCYTHE encodes the program as a typed declaration dependency graph and applies a set of semantic-aware operators that decouple declarations from their use sites, making them removable while keeping the program well-typed. Fine-grained token-level minimization is then left to the downstream reducer. On 73 benchmarks across C, Java, and Solidity, combining SCYTHE with PERSES never yields a larger result than PERSES alone, and a strictly smaller one on 70 of 73 cases. On average, the combination produces programs 55.6% smaller (up to 95.5%) and is 2.3$\times$ faster (up to 7.4$\times$). SCYTHE also boosts LATRA, a reducer that, unlike the purely syntactic PERSES, also applies language-specific transformations: the combination produces programs 10.6% smaller (up to 61.8%) and is 2.4$\times$ faster on average. Video: https://youtu.be/uEq_YYU0zZw

Software Engineering.title: HELIX: HEterogeneous LLM Inference with FleXible and Fine-Grained Partitioning
